explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The Spirit expressly states that in later times some will abandon the faith (1 Timothy 4:1). Paul isn't talking about a small stumble here. He's talking about people walking away.

Meeting together is a fine thing, friend, but that's not what the Spirit says in this verse. Paul says some will abandon the faith (1 Timothy 4:1). That's walking away from the faith itself, which is bigger than skipping a gathering.

Scripture matters a lot in this letter. Later in this very passage, Paul tells Timothy to devote himself to the public reading of Scripture (1 Timothy 4:13). But in verse 1, the Spirit says some will abandon the faith. Forgetting a book isn't the same as turning away.

You got it, baker. Paul says these people will prohibit marriage and require abstinence from certain foods (1 Timothy 4:3). Notice he's naming two things people will forbid, and neither one is something he tells believers to give up.

Nope, friend, prayer and songs aren't on this list. Paul says these people will prohibit marriage and require abstinence from certain foods (1 Timothy 4:3). Prayer actually shows up in the very next verses as part of what sanctifies things (1 Timothy 4:5).

Travel and festivals aren't on Paul's list, friend. He says these people will prohibit marriage and require abstinence from certain foods (1 Timothy 4:3). Neither travel nor festivals come up anywhere in these verses. The two things are marriage and certain foods.

That's the word, baker. Paul says God created those foods to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth (1 Timothy 4:3). Then he says nothing received with thanksgiving should be rejected (1 Timothy 4:4). Thanks goes with the gift.

Close to the topic, friend, but it's not the word Paul uses. He says God created those foods to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth (1 Timothy 4:3). The verse is about receiving, with thanks.

Careful there, friend, because Paul doesn't say caution. He says God created those foods to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth (1 Timothy 4:3). He's pointing to a thankful heart, not a nervous one.

That's right, baker. Paul says, "For every creation of God is good…" (1 Timothy 4:4). He goes on to say that nothing received with thanksgiving should be rejected. EVERY creation, friend. That's a big word, and it's the whole point.
Not quite, friend. Paul says, "For every creation of God is good…" (1 Timothy 4:4). Every one of them. And he adds that nothing received with thanksgiving should be rejected.

explanations.answer: The word of God and prayer
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Paul says what is received with thanksgiving is sanctified by the word of God and prayer (1 Timothy 4:5). Two things, and they're both about God and talking with Him. A thankful heart, God's word and prayer all go together here.

Paul doesn't mention a priest in these verses, friend. He says what is received with thanksgiving is sanctified by the word of God and prayer (1 Timothy 4:5). That's what he points to, and nothing else is on the list.

I'm all for clean hands in a bakery, friend, but that's not what Paul says. He says what is received with thanksgiving is sanctified by the word of God and prayer (1 Timothy 4:5). Those are the two things he names.

It's the other way around, baker. Paul says, "By pointing out these things to the brothers, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus…" (1 Timothy 4:6). Pointing them out is how Timothy serves. Keeping them to himself isn't in the verse.

Right, baker. Paul says, "By pointing out these things to the brothers, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus…" (1 Timothy 4:6). Timothy is meant to share them, and he's nourished by the words of faith and sound instruction he has followed. Keeping them to himself isn't in the verse.
That's it, baker. Paul says, "Instead, train yourself for godliness." (1 Timothy 4:7). Notice the word train. Godliness is something Timothy works at, like practice.
Good try, friend, but Paul doesn't say debate. He says to reject irreverent, silly myths and, "Instead, train yourself for godliness." (1 Timothy 4:7). The training is aimed at godliness.

Leadership is a fair guess, friend, since Paul left Timothy in Ephesus to do a job (1 Timothy 1:3). But Paul's word here is godliness. He says, "Instead, train yourself for godliness." (1 Timothy 4:7).

explanations.answer: It holds promise for this life and the next
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Paul says godliness is valuable in every way, "…holding promise for the present life and for the one to come." (1 Timothy 4:8). That's two lives covered. Not many things can say that.

explanations.answer: It keeps a person from all trouble
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't promise that, friend. He says godliness is valuable in every way, "…holding promise for the present life and for the one to come." (1 Timothy 4:8). The promise he names is for this life and the next.

explanations.answer: It earns respect from the elders
explanations.explanation: Elders do show up later in this passage, friend, when Paul mentions the laying on of hands (1 Timothy 4:14). But here Paul gives a different reason. Godliness is valuable because it holds promise for the present life and for the one to come (1 Timothy 4:8).

explanations.answer: Because we have set our hope on the living God
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, baker. Paul says, "To this end we labor and strive, because we have set our hope on the living God…" (1 Timothy 4:10). The hard work rests on that hope. He also calls Him the Savior of everyone, and especially of those who believe.

explanations.answer: Because the false teachers keep growing in number
explanations.explanation: Paul does warn about people who abandon the faith earlier in the passage, friend, but he doesn't give that as the reason here. He says, "To this end we labor and strive, because we have set our hope on the living God…" (1 Timothy 4:10). The reason is where the hope is set.

explanations.answer: Because the elders are watching over our work
explanations.explanation: Nobody's checking a clipboard in this verse, friend. Paul says, "To this end we labor and strive, because we have set our hope on the living God…" (1 Timothy 4:10). The reason is hope in the living God, and elders aren't mentioned here.
That's right, baker. Paul says, "Let no one despise your youth…" (1 Timothy 4:12). Timothy is young, and Paul doesn't tell him to hide it. He tells him what to do instead.

Ooh, digging into the past, friend? Paul doesn't go there in this verse. He says, "Let no one despise your youth…" (1 Timothy 4:12). Then he tells Timothy to set an example for the believers in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity.
Hometown doesn't come up in this verse, friend. Paul says, "Let no one despise your youth…" (1 Timothy 4:12). Timothy's youth is what's on the table.

Yes, baker. Right after he says not to let anyone despise Timothy's youth, Paul says, "…but set an example for the believers in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity." (1 Timothy 4:12). That's five places to lead by example. Paul gives him something to do about it.

Actually, friend, Paul does tell him that. He says, "Let no one despise your youth, but set an example for the believers in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity." (1 Timothy 4:12). Timothy's age doesn't cancel the assignment.

That's the word, baker. Paul says, "Until I come, devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, and to teaching." (1 Timothy 4:13). Reading it out loud for everyone comes first on the list.

Decrees sound official, friend, but that's not what Paul says. He says, "Until I come, devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, and to teaching." (1 Timothy 4:13). It's Scripture that gets read out loud.

Nobody's reading out the paperwork here, friend. Paul says, "Until I come, devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, and to teaching." (1 Timothy 4:13). The word he uses is Scripture.

explanations.answer: Through a prophecy as the elders laid hands on him
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. Paul says the gift "…was given you through the prophecy spoken over you at the laying on of the hands of the elders." (1 Timothy 4:14). A prophecy and the elders' hands, both together. Then Paul tells Timothy not to neglect it.

explanations.answer: Through a dream from an angel of the Lord
explanations.explanation: An angel visit would be a big story, friend, but Paul doesn't tell one here. He says the gift was given "…through the prophecy spoken over you at the laying on of the hands of the elders." (1 Timothy 4:14). That's how Timothy received it.

explanations.answer: Through a letter from the apostles in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Paul is the one writing the letter in this passage, friend, and he doesn't mention one from Jerusalem. He says the gift was given "…through the prophecy spoken over you at the laying on of the hands of the elders." (1 Timothy 4:14). That's the way it came.
You got it, baker. Paul says, "Be diligent in these matters and absorbed in them, so that your progress will be evident to all." (1 Timothy 4:15). Stay at it, and people can see the growth.

Humility is a good thing, friend, but it's not Paul's word here. He says, "Be diligent in these matters and absorbed in them, so that your progress will be evident to all." (1 Timothy 4:15). What shows is progress.

Rewards sound nice, friend, but that's not the word Paul picked. He says, "Be diligent in these matters and absorbed in them, so that your progress will be evident to all." (1 Timothy 4:15). Stay at it, and what everybody sees is progress. Like a batch rising in the oven, it shows.
Not so, baker. Paul says, "Pay close attention to your life and to your teaching." (1 Timothy 4:16). He puts life and teaching side by side, and he doesn't rank one above the other.

Right, baker. Paul says, "Pay close attention to your life and to your teaching." (1 Timothy 4:16). Both get close attention. I think a cookie that looks great and tastes like cardboard would teach the same lesson.

explanations.answer: Himself and those who hear him
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Paul says, "Persevere in these things, for by so doing you will save both yourself and those who hear you." (1 Timothy 4:16). Both Timothy and his listeners are in it together. Keep going, because it matters for more than one person.

explanations.answer: Himself and the elders who laid hands on him
explanations.explanation: The elders are mentioned earlier, friend, at the laying on of hands (1 Timothy 4:14), but not here. Paul says Timothy will "…save both yourself and those who hear you." (1 Timothy 4:16). It's the people who hear him.

explanations.answer: Those who hear him and their households
explanations.explanation: That one adds something Paul doesn't say, friend. He says, "…you will save both yourself and those who hear you." (1 Timothy 4:16). Timothy himself is named, and households aren't in the verse.
